prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, trapping atoms at a magic wavelength to reach fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a genuinely new idea with a clean physical core: choose the wavelength at which the ground and excited clock states have the same polarizability, and the trapping light stops shifting the transition. That removes Doppler and recoil effects and lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once. The proposal (Katori, 2001-2003) and the experimental push to the 1e-18 regime and to many-body clocks (Ye) are both clearly attributable, so a two-person prize is compact and fair. The result has been reproduced and surpassed in Tokyo, Boulder, Paris, Germany and China, with clock-to-clock comparisons agreeing at the 1e-18 level, which is the kind of robustness I look for. It has already delivered something nobody expected a few decades ago: relativistic redshift resolved across millimetres, new bounds on variation of constants and a route to redefining the second. It is a discovery about what quantum systems let us measure, not a technology prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is an instrument and precision-measurement achievement rather than the discovery of a new phenomenon, and that frequency metrology has already been honoured in 2005 (comb) and 2012 (control of single quantum systems, including the ion clock). A committee that wants a new phenomenon in nature could reasonably prefer topological insulators or twisted bilayer graphene. There is also an attribution point: other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto) made early and important contributions, and the split between the theoretical magic-wavelength idea and the Boulder realisation can be argued. Finally, I am close to this field and know its details well, which may bias me upward.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first as a new class of quantum matter that builds on the 2016 prize without repeating it, while ranking the lattice clock fourth and calling the overlap with earlier frequency-metrology prizes a possible incrementality worry.
responses.response: I take the topological case seriously and ranked B058 third myself; the Kane-Mele proposal followed by quick experimental confirmation is exactly the combination I like. I disagree on the overlap point. The 2005 prize honoured the comb and the 2012 prize honoured ion-trap control; neither covered neutral-atom trapping at a magic wavelength, which is a separate idea with its own physics, and the sensitivity gain is a thousandfold. Where I do agree is on attribution: the topological trio omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang for the HgTe route and the 3D work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Hasan, whereas the clock credit does not need a third name. That cleanliness is a practical reason to prefer B030 as the first configuration.

responses.point: Danielsson puts the CMB anisotropy mapping first as the foundation of precision cosmology, and IceCube second, while placing the lattice clock third as a clear invention with reach into fundamental physics and mature independent confirmation.
responses.response: I agree with his assessment of the clock, in particular that the millimetre-scale redshift tests and constant-variation limits give it real reach into fundamental physics, and that the redefinition of the second makes it timely. On B055 I defer to him on the science but not on the allocation: his own attribution paragraph concedes that the WMAP versus Planck split and the omission of Page and the instrument builders is a genuine problem, and the two opening ballots that carry it (his and Pearce's) propose different trios. That is an unresolved name set, not just a three-person limit squeezing a clear answer. I would need that settled before I could put it above a candidate whose credited names are agreed by all seven supporters.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and Cirac-Zoller second, arguing that Cirac and Zoller laid the theoretical foundation of two quantum-technology platforms and that the field is mature and arguably overdue, while declaring his own proximity to circuit QED.
responses.response: I share his high view of Cirac and Zoller, which is why I placed B044 second, and I welcome his frank statement of proximity on B029. My qualification is that B044 is a prize for theory, and I would want the citation to say so plainly and to separate the 1995 ion-gate proposal from the lattice-simulation work, as he notes the decisive paper differs between the parts. The experimental realisations belong to Wineland, Blatt, Monroe and the cold-atom groups, and Wineland is already recognised in 2012. On B029, with the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits so recent, and Wallraff missing from the credited names, I would be reluctant to go back to superconducting circuits this soon, though I accept that the science is strong.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as a measurement instrument that changed what can be measured, notes that Ye was not a laureate in 2005, and flags the framing question of whether the prize is for the clock or for the magic-wavelength trapping idea.
responses.response: I agree on the strength of the case and on his point that Ye was not a 2005 laureate. On framing, I would cite the lattice trapping at the magic wavelength and its realisation in clocks together, because the idea is what is new and the clock is what shows it works; a citation for the clock alone would blur the line to the comb and ion-clock prizes. I also want to be careful about the persuasiveness of our agreement: we are both atomic physicists, and the members who rank it lower (Pearce fifth, Olsson eighth) may be reacting to a real concern that the discovery content is more metrological than conceptual, which I would like to hear spelled out.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards a precision-measurement invention as sufficient 'discovery' content given the 2005 and 2012 prizes in neighbouring metrology.
How to weigh the early contributions of other lattice-clock groups against the Katori and Ye pairing.
Whether the WMAP/Planck name set for B055 and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission for B058 can be resolved, since either would change how I rank those candidates.
The maturity of the redefinition of the second is still pending; I regard that as timing, not a weakness of the science.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, but none of those people is credited on any shortlisted ballot. I have no personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye, Cirac, Zoller, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp that appears in my profile; my proximity is only disciplinary, as an atomic physicist who knows lattice-clock physics well. No specific recusal conflict is apparent from the provided profile.
